name: Central Water Catchment
blurb: Zero HDB blocks, zero coffee shops, and the only planning area where most of the residents have tails. The whole Mandai wildlife precinct is in here, Zoo and Night Safari included, which surprises everyone who assumes it belongs to the area next door. Weekends belong to the MacRitchie boardwalk and the TreeTop Walk, 250 metres of swaying suspension bridge that quickly separates the confident from the quiet.
hint: Sprawling green block between Bukit Timah and Upper Thomson, no houses.
fact: The reserve spans about 2,880 hectares and holds four reservoirs: MacRitchie, Upper Peirce, Lower Peirce and Upper Seletar.

name: Yishun
blurb: Yishun has carried the cursed label since the 2015 cat killings went viral and the internet has never once let it go. The daily reality is Northpoint City queues on a Saturday and Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, which has more greenery than most condos and a koi pond people visit on purpose. The monitor lizards at the pond are the length of a bicycle and give way to nobody sia.
hint: Between Sembawang and Ang Mo Kio on the North-South MRT Line.
fact: Yishun is named after rubber and pineapple magnate Lim Nee Soon, whose name in Mandarin reads Lin Yi Shun.

name: Sungei Kadut
blurb: Nobody lives here. It is timber yards, furniture warehouses and lorries queuing at the weighbridge, the kind of place you only visit when your sofa finally gives out. Uncles used to make the trip for the horses at Kranji, but the Turf Club ran its last race in October 2024 and the grandstand has been shut ever since. Come for a rattan set at half what town charges, not for a day out.
hint: West of Woodlands, hugging Kranji Reservoir and the BKE.
fact: Singapore Turf Club held its final horse race at Kranji Racecourse on 5 October 2024.

name: Lim Chu Kang
blurb: The last proper farmland in Singapore is out here: vegetable plots, fish farms and a goat dairy strung along one two-lane road. Hay Dairies lets you watch the milking in the morning and Bollywood Veggies grows bananas by the acre, which is about as ulu as this country gets before you hit the sea. There is no MRT within striking distance, so if your ride cancels you are walking a very long way.
hint: Northwest coast facing the Strait of Johor, past Kranji.
fact: Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve, on its coast, became Singapore's first ASEAN Heritage Park in 2003.

name: Woodlands
blurb: The Causeway jam is a local sport: check the traffic cam, decide it looks clear, then sit in it for ninety minutes anyway. Friday evening the queue backs up past the checkpoint and everybody just accepts it lah, because Johor is right there and the ringgit is what it is. Away from the bridge it is Causeway Point, the long slides at Admiralty Park, and the fishing uncles at Woodlands Waterfront with a clear view of another country.
hint: Singapore's northern tip, linked to Johor Bahru by the Causeway.
fact: The Johor-Singapore Causeway linking Woodlands to Johor Bahru officially opened on 28 June 1924.

name: Sembawang
blurb: The British ran their naval base here, King George VI Dry Dock and all, the largest in the world when it opened in 1938, then handed the lot over for a token one dollar in 1968. The black and white officers' bungalows still line the old roads, rented out and quietly expensive, and Sembawang Park keeps the last stretch of natural beach on the north coast. The hot spring everybody associates with the name is actually across the boundary in Mandai.
hint: North coast next to Woodlands, on the North-South MRT line.
fact: The former British naval base at Sembawang was handed to Singapore in 1968 for a token one dollar.

name: Mandai
blurb: Everybody thinks this is where the zoo is. It is not: the Zoo, Night Safari, River Wonders and Bird Paradise all sit just over the line in the Central Water Catchment. What Mandai actually holds is a furniture and industrial estate, the road everybody drives through to get to the animals, and, against all reason, Sembawang Hot Spring Park.
hint: North-central strip along the road to the wildlife parks.
fact: Sembawang Hot Spring Park lies inside the Mandai planning area, not Sembawang.

name: Simpang
blurb: Simpang was meant to be a new town. The plan got shelved decades ago and the land went to the army and the mangroves instead, so the resident count has sat at zero for as long as anyone can remember. What is left is field camp country: shell scrapes, mudflats at low tide, and a stretch of coast facing Johor that almost nobody has ever walked.
hint: North of Yishun, between Sembawang and Seletar, facing the Strait.
fact: Plans for a Simpang New Town were shelved, leaving the area an SAF training ground with no permanent residents.

name: Western Water Catchment
blurb: You are not getting in, and that is rather the point. Tengeh, Poyan, Murai and Sarimbun quietly top up the national water supply behind a perimeter fence, a live firing area and signs every hundred metres telling you to turn around. The only people who ever see it properly are reservists on night navigation at 3am, and they are not looking at the scenery.
hint: Fenced reservoirs and army camps between Tuas and Choa Chu Kang.
fact: Home to four reservoirs, Tengeh, Poyan, Murai and Sarimbun, supplying part of Singapore's water.

name: Tuas
blurb: Everything the island would rather not look at happens out here: container yards, incineration plants, chemical tanks, and the Second Link running straight into Johor. Tuas Port is being built to swallow every other container terminal in the country by the 2040s, fully automated, driverless trucks and cranes worked from a control room somewhere else. Nobody comes here on purpose unless they work here or they are driving to Malaysia.
hint: Far southwest tip, linked to Johor by the Second Link bridge.
fact: Tuas Port began operations in 2022 and is designed to handle 65 million containers a year when fully complete.

name: Western Islands
blurb: Do not pack a towel, these are refinery islands. Jurong Island was stitched together from seven smaller ones into the third-largest oil refining centre on the planet, Pulau Bukom ran Shell's biggest wholly owned refinery for decades until Shell sold the lot in 2025, and Pulau Semakau doubles as the country's only landfill and, oddly, a decent birdwatching spot. You need a permit to set foot on most of it, so no chope-ing a beach here.
hint: Jurong Island and Pulau Bukom, offshore refineries, permit required.
fact: Jurong Island, formed by joining seven islands, is home to the world's third-largest oil refining centre.

name: Pioneer
blurb: Named for the industrial pioneers, staffed today by shipyard welders and technicians waiting on the last bus out. NTU sits just over the boundary, so the same stretch of road carries undergrads heading to lecture and men heading into a dry dock. There are more crane booms on the skyline here than HDB blocks, by a wide margin.
hint: Southwest coastal industrial belt beside NTU, below Jurong West.
fact: Jurong Industrial Estate, which includes Pioneer, was launched in 1961 as Singapore's first major industrial project.

name: Boon Lay
blurb: Jurong Bird Park sat on Jurong Hill here for over 50 years before packing up for Mandai in 2023, and a whole generation still hears this name and pictures flamingos and the penguin feed. What is actually on the ground now is shipyards, dry docks and factories, because the Boon Lay everyone shops and eats at, MRT station included, is technically next door in Jurong West. Barely anybody lives inside the real boundary, which makes this the rare town centre that exists somewhere else entirely.
hint: Industrial coast south of Jurong West, shipyards and the old bird park.
fact: Jurong Bird Park operated in Boon Lay for over 50 years until its closure in January 2023.

name: Tengah
blurb: The first town here planned with its roads tucked under the town centre, and with a forest corridor 100 metres wide cutting through the middle so the wildlife gets its own right of way. Right now half of it is still hoarding, cranes and red dust on your windscreen, with the first keys handed over in 2023. Ask anyone who collected early and you will get three years of stories about eating dinner inside a construction site.
hint: Forest town between Choa Chu Kang and Jurong, west of Bukit Batok.
fact: Tengah is Singapore's first HDB town planned with a car-free town centre and a 100-metre-wide forest corridor.

name: Choa Chu Kang
blurb: Lot One sits right on top of the MRT and LRT interchange and does the job for everyone from Yew Tee down to Keat Hong, which covers most of what daily life here involves. The name also belongs to the last cemetery in Singapore still taking burials, 318 hectares of it just over the boundary in the Western Water Catchment, where a grave gets 15 years before it is exhumed and the plot reused. Space is space lah, even for the dead.
hint: North of Bukit Batok, next to the new Tengah forest town.
fact: Choa Chu Kang Cemetery, open since 1947, is Singapore's only cemetery still accepting new burials.

name: Jurong East
blurb: Three malls in a row off one interchange, Westgate, JEM and IMM, the last of which people drive across the island for purely because of the outlet stores. JCube and its Olympic-size rink closed in 2023 to make way for a condo, which tells you exactly which way the wind is blowing. The plan is a second CBD, and Jurong Lake Gardens plus Ng Teng Fong hospital are the instalments that have actually landed.
hint: Western regional centre with three malls off one MRT interchange.
fact: JCube shopping mall, home to Singapore's first Olympic-size ice rink, permanently closed on 6 August 2023.

name: Jurong West
blurb: Jurong Point on a Sunday is the proof of scale: the basement food court queue doubles back on itself and the carpark tailback starts on the expressway ramp. Boon Lay MRT out front is where half the west transfers to somewhere else. Behind it the estate runs block after block on a numbering system that has defeated every delivery rider who has ever tried it lah.
hint: Singapore's far west heartland, south of Tengah, next to Boon Lay.
fact: Jurong West has about 254,000 residents, one of Singapore's largest HDB towns, though Tampines is the most populous planning area.

name: Bukit Batok
blurb: Little Guilin is an abandoned granite quarry that filled with water, and the name came from people who decided the rock face and the still lake were close enough to the real thing. Up the hill, 121 concrete steps still climb to nothing: the Japanese put a shrine at the top in 1942 and demolished it themselves before the surrender. The steps are the only part left, which makes for a very strange lunchtime walk.
hint: West-side town with a flooded granite quarry called Little Guilin.
fact: The Syonan Chureito war memorial atop Bukit Batok hill was consecrated by Japanese forces in September 1942.

name: Clementi
blurb: By 7:15 on a weekday the queue outside the station is forty students deep, all waiting on the NUS shuttle with one hand round a bubble tea. The mall above the interchange was HDB's first attempt at stacking flats, shops and buses into a single building back in 2011, and every integrated hub since has copied the homework. The 448 market next door does duck rice shiok enough to skip the mall for, but the students never look that far.
hint: East-West Line stop between Dover and Jurong East, near NUS.
fact: Clementi Mall, opened in 2011, was HDB's first development combining public housing, retail and a bus interchange.

name: Bukit Panjang
blurb: This is the area that quietly owns the highest ground in Singapore: Bukit Timah Hill, all 163.63 metres of it, and the nature reserve around it are both inside Bukit Panjang, not the area they are named after. Down at street level it is the LRT taking the scenic route to Senja in a single carriage, with Hillion Mall stacked on top of the interchange.
hint: Downtown Line terminus with its own LRT loop, near Choa Chu Kang.
fact: Bukit Timah Hill, 163.63 metres and Singapore's highest natural point, sits in the Bukit Panjang planning area.

name: Queenstown
blurb: Built from 1952 by the Singapore Improvement Trust, before HDB existed, this was the country's first satellite town. What survives is three eras in one postcode: the last walk-ups near Tanglin Halt with laundry poles out the windows, the Dawson towers with sky gardens bolted on, and one-north where the biotech labs are. The library on Margaret Drive, opened in 1970, was the first branch library Singapore ever built.
hint: West of Bukit Merah, wrapping Kent Ridge and one-north.
fact: Queenstown was developed from 1952 as Singapore's first satellite housing town, named after Queen Elizabeth II's coronation.

name: Bukit Timah
blurb: The hill is not here. Bukit Timah Hill and the nature reserve sit next door in Bukit Panjang, which catches out almost everybody. What this area actually is: the Good Class Bungalow belt, embassy hedging along Holland Road, Sixth Avenue, and Beauty World Centre still doing a roaring trade in cai fan under a shopping centre nobody has ever called new.
hint: Central area around Singapore's highest hill, near Holland Road.
fact: Bukit Timah Hill and Bukit Timah Nature Reserve fall inside the Bukit Panjang planning area, not Bukit Timah.

name: North-Eastern Islands
blurb: Rent a bicycle with a rusted chain at the Ubin jetty and the clock rolls back forty years: zinc roofs, durian trees, and uncles checking the German Girl Shrine for 4D numbers. Tekong next door is where every 18 year old male citizen gets shipped for basic training, so half the country has a story about that ferry ride and none of them are happy ones. Between the two, the emptiest and greenest corner of Singapore. Mud, mangrove, mosquitoes.
hint: Reached by bumboat from Changi Point, near Johor Strait.
fact: Pulau Ubin's Chek Jawa wetlands, slated for reclamation in 1992, was saved after a 2001 public campaign.

name: Ang Mo Kio
blurb: Lee Hsien Loong has been the MP here since 1991, which means a sitting Prime Minister ran a Meet-the-People session in this estate every week for two decades. The town is 1970s vintage, the seventh HDB built, and it shows in the wide void decks and the rain trees that have had fifty years to fill out. AMK Hub sits on the interchange and absorbs the entire town the moment it rains.
hint: Heartland town north of Bishan and south of Yio Chu Kang.
fact: Ang Mo Kio New Town's construction began in 1973, making it the seventh HDB satellite town built in Singapore.

name: Hougang
blurb: The Workers' Party has held this seat since 1991, longer than any opposition ward in the country, and the blue flags come out every election like a monsoon. It has stayed low-rise and old-school: Hougang Mall, the stadium where the Cheetahs play to a few hundred loyalists, and coffee shops where people will tell you exactly how they voted and why. The building boom went straight past to Punggol, and residents count that as a win.
hint: Between Serangoon and Punggol, along the Kallang-Paya Lebar Expressway.
fact: Workers' Party's Low Thia Khiang won Hougang SMC in 1991, starting an opposition hold that continues today.

name: Seletar
blurb: Singapore's first airport opened here in 1930 for the RAF, and the runway is still working almost a century later, now handling private jets and flying school circuits. Rolls-Royce assembles Trent engines a few hundred metres from the taxiway, in a business park sharing a fence line with the airfield. The colonial bungalows on the old base estate stay rented, quiet and lined with rain trees, and hardly any bus route bothers going in.
hint: North coast facing Johor Strait, between Yishun and Punggol.
fact: Seletar Airport opened in 1930 as Singapore's first airport, initially built for the Royal Air Force.

name: Sengkang
blurb: Every second young couple in Singapore seems to start married life here, so the lifts run full of strollers and the playgrounds fill up by five. The LRT loops through Rivervale, Compassvale and Anchorvale, proof that somebody at the planning office picked a theme and absolutely refused to drop it. Compass One handles the shopping and Sengkang General handles the deliveries, sometimes for the same household in the same year sia.
hint: Northeast new town split by two looping light-rail lines, near Punggol.
fact: Sengkang General Hospital opened in August 2018, serving the fast-growing northeast region.

name: Serangoon
blurb: Chomp Chomp has been doing barbecued sotong and carrot cake since 1972 and still draws a queue at 9pm on a Tuesday. Cash only, find your own table, expect no sympathy. Ten minutes away the landed houses of the Gardens give out and it becomes HDB blocks and NEX, the mall that captured the whole northeast's weekend traffic when it opened in 2010.
hint: Where the North East Line meets the Circle Line, near Bishan.
fact: Chomp Chomp Food Centre in Serangoon Gardens has served hawker food since 1972.

name: Punggol
blurb: Twenty years ago the only reason to come out this far was seafood at the end of the road and prawning off the jetty. Now there is a 4.2 km waterway with joggers on both banks, BTO blocks going up faster than the map can keep up with, and a digital district with a university campus folded into it. Punggol Point itself stays quiet, which suits it: Japanese troops shot several hundred Chinese men on that beach in February 1942.
hint: Northeastern coastal new town, waterway park facing the Johor Strait.
fact: Around 300 to 400 Chinese civilians were killed by Japanese forces at Punggol Point in February 1942.

name: Toa Payoh
blurb: The first town HDB planned and built from nothing, ground broken in 1964, and every heartland since has copied the layout: town centre in the middle, blocks radiating out, market and hawker centre within walking distance. The dragon at Lorong 6 is the last one still sitting in sand, and the kids who scraped their knees on it in the 90s now bring their own children down. HDB still runs its headquarters here, a bit like an architect refusing to move out of the first house he built.
hint: South of Bishan, central town with HDB's headquarters inside.
fact: Toa Payoh, HDB's first satellite town planned and built entirely from scratch, broke ground in 1964.

name: Bishan
blurb: The whole town sits on Peck San Theng, a Cantonese burial ground where more than 75,000 graves were exhumed between 1982 and 1984 to clear the land for flats. Every seventh month somebody at the coffee shop brings it up again, everybody nods, and everybody keeps eating. Above ground it is Junction 8, Raffles Institution, and Bishan Park, where the concrete canal was ripped out and rebuilt as a river, otters included.
hint: Sandwiched between Ang Mo Kio and Toa Payoh, along the Kallang River.
fact: More than 75,000 graves at the Peck San Theng cemetery were exhumed between 1982 and 1984 for Bishan New Town.

name: Changi
blurb: Tell a Singaporean that someone got sent here and nobody pictures the airport, because the prison has been down the road since 1936 and spent the war holding interned civilians. The other side of it is the village at the end of the bus route: a nasi lemak queue that eats forty minutes of your evening, the bumboat jetty to Ubin, and a beach facing entirely the wrong way for sunsets. Two kilometres apart, three different worlds.
hint: Singapore's eastern tip, beyond the airport runways, ferry to Ubin.
fact: Changi Airport's Terminal 1 opened in 1981, ending Paya Lebar's run as Singapore's main airport.

name: Bedok
blurb: Bedok Reservoir was a sand quarry until they let it flood, and it is now one of the few places you can legally drop a line, so the loop carries joggers going one way and anglers going nowhere at all. Bedok Corner is still doing its supper trade under the same open-air roof, sambal stingray past midnight, regulars who have not changed tables in twenty years. The town is big enough that two MRT lines run through it and it is still all Bedok sia.
hint: Wedged between Marine Parade and Tampines, big reservoir at its heart.
fact: Bedok Reservoir was created from a disused sand quarry and completed around 1986 as a water supply reservoir.

name: Tampines
blurb: The first regional centre Singapore built, and it still looks the part: three malls facing each other across one junction, plus a library, a stadium and a swimming complex folded into Our Tampines Hub. IKEA out here is the unofficial Sunday programme for half the east, meatballs first, furniture maybe. The cycling paths arrived a decade before the rest of the island got round to it, which is why everyone rides on the pavement and nobody stops them.
hint: Far east interior, near Pasir Ris and Bedok, first regional hub.
fact: Our Tampines Hub, Singapore's first integrated community and sports hub, officially opened in 2017.

name: Pasir Ris
blurb: The mangrove boardwalk comes with a macaque troop that has worked out how to open a Ziploc bag, so keep yours shut and your hands on it. Downtown East has run the school holiday programme since the chalets opened in 1988, and Wild Wild Wet joined in 2004 to give every east-side kid the same photo on the same water slide. White Sands is small and nobody from outside the estate ever goes there, which the estate considers a feature rather than a flaw.
hint: Coastal strip between Tampines and Changi, monkeys included.
fact: NTUC's Downtown East opened in 1988 as Singapore's largest seaside resort, with 396 chalets.

name: Paya Lebar
blurb: This was Singapore's international airport until Changi took over in 1981, and the air base that stayed behind still caps how tall anything nearby is allowed to be built. The glassy Paya Lebar Quarter towers that borrow the name actually sit one planning area west, in Geylang, so what is genuinely here is runway, hangars and the Airport Road industrial stretch. Come July the flypast rehearsals go over and the whole neighbourhood looks up out of pure habit.
hint: East of Hougang, north of Bedok, almost entirely an air base.
fact: Paya Lebar Airport opened in 1955 and served as Singapore's main airport until Changi opened in 1981.

name: Changi Bay
blurb: Changi Naval Base, the SAF Yacht Club, and a park connector running out to the easternmost point of mainland Singapore. That is the complete list. Nearly all of it is reclaimed, so the ground under your wheels was seabed within living memory, and the cyclists who ride out here do it precisely because nobody else does.
hint: Easternmost reclaimed sliver past the airport, naval base, no residents.
fact: Changi Bay covers about 1.7 sq km of mostly reclaimed land and has no permanent residents.

name: Geylang
blurb: The odd and even lorong split is the unofficial map every local carries: one side for the food, the other for the trade nobody names out loud. Lorong 9 does frog leg porridge past midnight and the durian stalls along the main road stay open long after the rest of the island has shut. Round the corner Geylang Serai runs the Hari Raya bazaar every year, so the same stretch holds festival lights and a licensed vice trade and nobody finds it worth remarking on.
hint: Between Kallang and Marine Parade, dozens of numbered lorongs off one road.
fact: An island-wide anti-vice campaign in August 1959 pushed brothel operators into Geylang's even-numbered lorongs; it was designated a red-light area in 1998.

name: Marine Parade
blurb: Katong laksa starts arguments here, mostly about which shop is the original and who earned the right to cut the noodles short enough to eat with a spoon. Parkway Parade has anchored the place since 1984 and is somehow busy on a Tuesday afternoon, largely with people who have been coming for forty years. East Coast Park runs the entire southern edge, where the 6am cyclists ride in packs and treat the crossings as advisory.
hint: Reclaimed coastal strip south of Geylang, condos facing East Coast Park.
fact: Parkway Parade, one of Singapore's earliest large suburban malls, opened on 9 March 1984.

name: Kallang
blurb: The Kallang Wave started in the old stadium, a stand-up cheer that rolled round the terraces every time the national team looked like scoring, which was not often. Long before the football, this was Singapore's first civil airport, opened in 1937, with Amelia Earhart putting down on that runway eight days later. Up the road, Golden Mile Complex was Little Thailand until the shops cleared out in 2023, and it now sits behind hoarding waiting to reopen as something with a higher price per square foot.
hint: River mouth west of Geylang, home to the National Stadium.
fact: Kallang Airport, Singapore's first civil airport, opened in 1937; Amelia Earhart landed there eight days later.

name: Bukit Merah
blurb: Tiong Bahru's 1930s walk-ups now hold sourdough bakeries and a bird corner where the same uncles hang their merbok cages every Sunday morning, each side ignoring the other completely. Henderson Waves crosses 36 metres above the road between Mount Faber and Telok Blangah Hill, the highest pedestrian bridge in the country and worth the climb at dusk. At the bottom of the same hill sit VivoCity and the cable car station, all inside one planning area.
hint: East of Queenstown along the harbour, VivoCity and Mount Faber inside.
fact: Henderson Waves, opened in 2008, is Singapore's highest pedestrian bridge at 36 metres above the road below.

name: Novena
blurb: This is a hospital district with a mall attached: Tan Tock Seng, Mount Elizabeth Novena and the rest of the HealthCity precinct, stitched together with link bridges so nobody has to cross the road on foot. United Square is known to every parent as the enrichment mothership, floor after floor of tuition, ballet and abacus. Square 2 connects straight into the hospital, so visiting hours and dinner get handled in one trip.
hint: North of Newton, straddling the Central Expressway near Moulmein Road.
fact: Tan Tock Seng Hospital, founded in 1844 by philanthropist Tan Tock Seng, is one of Singapore's oldest hospitals.

name: Tanglin
blurb: Half the embassies in Singapore sit behind these hedges, and Dempsey Hill will charge you forty dollars for a salad in what used to be British Army barracks built over a nutmeg plantation. The Botanic Gardens open at Tanglin Gate right on the boundary, the oldest corner of a garden that has been running since 1859. On a Sunday morning the car park is all Defenders and Range Rovers, and the dogs get out first.
hint: West of Orchard, wraps around the Botanic Gardens' eastern flank.
fact: Singapore Botanic Gardens became Singapore's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015 and spans about 82 hectares.

name: Southern Islands
blurb: Sentosa takes the tourists and the cable car fares, and the outer islands take everyone trying to get away from the tourists. Kusu has a turtle sanctuary and a Chinese temple that draws tens of thousands of pilgrims every ninth lunar month, most of them asking for the same two things. St John's ran as a quarantine station from 1874 and later as an opium treatment centre, and is now campsites, feral cats and a jetty with nothing on it.
hint: Ferry from the mainland to Sentosa, Kusu and St John's.
fact: St John's Island operated as a quarantine station from 1874, and by 1935 could hold about 6,000 people across 22 camps.

name: Downtown Core
blurb: Suits above ground and an entire second city below it: the underground malls run from Raffles Place to Marina Bay, so you can cross the whole financial district in a thunderstorm without seeing daylight or getting wet. Marina Bay Sands has been photographed from the same three angles by every visitor since 2010 and the infinity pool queue has never once got shorter. Money has been made on this exact spot since Collyer Quay was a working waterfront. Only the glass is new.
hint: Where the Singapore River meets the sea, ringed by skyscrapers.
fact: Marina Bay Sands opened in 2010 with a 150-metre rooftop infinity pool spanning its three towers.

name: Newton
blurb: More interchange than neighbourhood, a knot of flyovers where the PIE meets the CTE, with almost nobody living inside the boundary. The food centre at the circus has been sending tourists home with satay since 1971, and in 2009 one stall billed six American visitors 491 dollars for a single seafood dinner and lost its licence for three months over it. Locals still turn up, mostly late, mostly for the oyster omelette.
hint: A small road interchange wedged between Novena, Orchard and the Museum area.
fact: Newton Food Centre opened in 1971 as one of Singapore's earliest purpose-built hawker centres.

name: Marina East
blurb: The half of Gardens by the Bay with no Supertrees, and therefore no crowds, is out here, sharing the land with a golf course and a desalination plant. All of it was seabed until reclamation filled it in, and the master plan for whatever comes next keeps getting pushed further down the road. For now it is the only stretch of Marina waterfront where you can run three kilometres without passing a single tour group.
hint: Reclaimed land beside Gardens by the Bay, golf course inside.
fact: The Marina East Desalination Plant, Singapore's fourth, opened in 2020 and can produce 30 million gallons daily.

name: Marina South
blurb: The pier here is where the bumboats leave for the offshore islands, and that is currently the entire reason to make the trip. The land was reclaimed decades ago and then left alone, so it is flat plots with road markings painted on them, waiting on 10,000 homes that exist only on a URA map. The rest is carpark and empty roads smooth enough to take a driving test on.
hint: Southern tip of the reclaimed bay, where island ferries depart.
fact: Marina South Pier, opened in 2006, is the departure point for ferries to Singapore's Southern Islands.

name: Straits View
blurb: At 0.77 square kilometres this is the smallest planning area in Singapore, narrower across than most people's walk to the MRT. It came out of the Marina City reclamation in the 1980s and has spent the forty years since as hoarding, holding ground and a road or two. On paper it is the link between the Downtown Core and the Greater Southern Waterfront, which is considerable ambition for a plot you can cross in fifteen minutes.
hint: Sliver of reclaimed coast between Marina South and the Downtown Core.
fact: Straits View is Singapore's smallest planning area at 0.77 square kilometres, created during the 1980s Marina City reclamation.

name: Rochor
blurb: Tekka Centre, Sultan Mosque and Haji Lane all sit within a fifteen minute walk, which means Little India and Kampong Glam are technically the same planning area. Sim Lim Square is where you go to haggle for a laptop, and where a generation of tourists learned an expensive lesson about deposits. Sungei Road's Thieves' Market, the oldest flea market in Singapore, ran here until 2017 before the land was wanted for something with a better yield.
hint: Between Newton and the Downtown Core, north of the Museum district.
fact: Sungei Road Thieves' Market, Singapore's oldest flea market, permanently closed on 10 July 2017.

name: River Valley
blurb: Zouk ran out of a converted godown on Jiak Kim Street from 1991 to 2016, and for twenty-five years this riverbank was where the country came to lose a Saturday night. The warehouses are conserved now, wrapped in a condo, and the address gets sold on the promise that you can walk to Orchard and walk to the water. Great World holds the other end, and after midnight the loudest thing on the street is the taxi queue.
hint: Between Orchard and the water, anchored by Great World mall.
fact: Zouk nightclub operated on Jiak Kim Street here from 1991 to 2016, before moving to a new home downstream.

name: Outram
blurb: Singapore General Hospital has been treating people on this stretch of Outram Road since 1882, and the campus has grown until it takes up most of the planning area. Around it sit People's Park Complex and its brutalist slab, Pearl's Hill above the old police lines, and shophouses that have been dim sum restaurants for three generations. Sri Mariamman Temple on South Bridge Road got here first, in 1827, and its gopuram still stops traffic.
hint: Below the Singapore River, wraps around People's Park and Pearl's Hill.
fact: Sri Mariamman Temple on South Bridge Road, Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, was founded in 1827 by Naraina Pillai.

name: Orchard
blurb: A little over two kilometres of malls built on top of the nutmeg and pepper orchards that gave the road its name. ION and Tangs hold one end, Emerald Hill's Peranakan shophouses hold the other, and the stretch in between changes its shopfronts faster than anyone can keep track of. Every tourist photograph of Singapore that is not Marina Bay was taken somewhere on this street.
hint: Singapore's main shopping belt between Tanglin and Newton, Istana inside.
fact: Tangs department store, founded in 1932 by C.K. Tang, still anchors Orchard Road with its distinctive green-tiled roof.

name: Singapore River
blurb: Three kilometres of water and three separate crowds: Boat Quay's shophouse bars catch the after-work CBD, Clarke Quay does neon and bottle service, and Robertson Quay upstream does brunch with a pram parked alongside. This was the working harbour, bumboats hauling rubber and tin to the godowns, until the clean-up through the 1980s moved the whole trade out for good. You can walk from the mouth to Kim Seng Bridge and never be more than fifty metres from a drink.
hint: The waterway linking Robertson Quay to Marina Bay through the Downtown Core.
fact: The Singapore River stretches about 3 kilometres from Kim Seng Bridge to the sea at Marina Bay.

name: Museum
blurb: The National Museum, the Art Museum and Fort Canning Hill sit inside one small block, which makes this the closest thing Singapore has to a civic quarter. Under the hill is the Battle Box, the bunker where Percival and his commanders decided to surrender on 15 February 1942, now open to visitors with the room laid out the way it was left. Below that, Bras Basah runs on art students and second-hand bookshops instead of retail chains.
hint: Between Orchard and the civic district, built around Fort Canning Hill.
fact: At Fort Canning's Battle Box bunker, British commanders agreed to surrender Singapore to Japan on 15 February 1942.
